Let $f(x)=-4{x}^{4}-26{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-4x+21.$ We know that $(x-1)$ and $(x+7)$ are factors of $f(x),$ and we need to find its other factors.

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $f(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{4}$ | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-4$ | $-26$ | $13$ | $-4$ | $21$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-4$ | $-30$ | $-17$ | $-21$ |
|  | $-4$ | $-30$ | $-17$ | $-21$ | $0$ |

Therefore,  

$$
\frac{-4{x}^{4}-26{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-4x+21}{x-1}=-4{x}^{3}-30{x}^{2}-17x-21,
$$

which means that  

$$
-4{x}^{4}-26{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-4x+21=(x-1)(-4{x}^{3}-30{x}^{2}-17x-21).
$$

Now, because $(x+7)$ is also a factor of $f(x),$ it must be a factor of the quotient $(-4{x}^{3}-30{x}^{2}-17x-21).$ So, we divide this quotient by $(x+7)$ using synthetic division once more:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-7$ | $-4$ | $-30$ | $-17$ | $-21$ |
|  | $↓$ | $28$ | $14$ | $21$ |
|  | $-4$ | $-2$ | $-3$ | $0$ |

Therefore,  

$$
\frac{-4{x}^{3}-30{x}^{2}-17x-25}{x+7}=-4{x}^{2}-2x-3,
$$

which means that  

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{4}-26{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-4x+21 & =(x-1)(x+7)(-4{x}^{2}-2x-3) \\  & =-(x-1)(x+7)(4{x}^{2}+2x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

To see whether the quadratic polynomial $4{x}^{2}+2x+3$ can be factored any further, we calculate its discriminant:  

$$
{b}^{2}-4ac=(2)^{2}-4(4)(3)=-44<0.
$$

So, the quadratic polynomial $4{x}^{2}+2x+3$ cannot be factored over the real numbers since its discriminant is negative.  

Therefore, the full factorization of $f(x)$ over the real numbers is given by  

$$
-4{x}^{4}-26{x}^{3}+13{x}^{2}-4x+21=-(x-1)(x+7){{(4{x}^{2}+2x+3)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}.
$$

Finally, $P(x)=4{x}^{2}+2x+3.$
